routes.description: Establish that neither deterministic causation nor indeterministic chance supplies the ultimate authorship or identical-circumstances alternatives associated with libertarian freedom, and that practical agency and accountability do not restore those missing features.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if causal dependence and preconscious formation exclude ultimate authorship, randomness cannot repair that exclusion, and useful responsibility practices can be retained without treating agents as metaphysically self-originating.

motionBridge.description: Show that determinism and indeterminism both fail to provide ultimate authorship, so reasons-responsive competence cannot preserve free will in the disputed first-person sense.

centralBridges.description: Establish that authorship and a genuine ability to do otherwise are indispensable to the free-will concept at issue rather than dispensable supernatural additions.
Show that thoughts, intentions, character, and decisive neural conditions arise from prior causes the agent did not choose or ultimately author.
Separate pragmatic accountability, deterrence, and protection from ultimate desert, allowing useful social practices without metaphysical self-authorship.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use prospective neural or behavioral prediction to test whether consciousness originates action or becomes aware only after its causal formation.
Explain why fuller causal knowledge of impairment, character, or anomalous conduct tends to recast blameworthy action as an intelligible condition.

routes.description: Establish that the freedom relevant to moral responsibility consists in naturalistic, reasons-responsive capacities for self-control, planning, and action across real practical alternatives, none of which requires causal independence or quantum indeterminacy.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if reasons-responsive competence supports meaningful authorship and alternative possibilities, relevant differences between capable and impaired agents survive universal causation, and responsibility practices remain justified by those capacities and their social functions.

motionBridge.description: Show that reasons-responsive agency supplies the morally relevant freedom worth preserving and remains fully compatible with deterministic causation.

centralBridges.description: Justify retaining a naturalistic free-will concept after removing absolute self-creation, magical control, and morally irrelevant indeterminacy.
Ground authorship and control in temporally extended capacities to deliberate, plan, learn, regulate conduct, and respond competently to reasons.
Explain the ability to do otherwise through an agent's real range of competences and relevant counterfactual variation rather than atom-for-atom replay.
Connect differences in agency capacity to reasonable expectations, excuses, obligations, sanctions, and cooperative legal and moral practices.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish retrospective neural decoding from actionable foreknowledge and identify limits on predictions that interact with the predicted agent.
Account for chance and inherited conditions without requiring agents to control every causal input to exercise responsible self-regulation.

sections.title: The Concept and Subject Matter of Free Will
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether naturalistic refinement preserves the disputed concept or replaces indispensable first-person authorship and alternative possibility with a different account of agency.

sections.title: Authorship, Conscious Awareness, and Control
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether unconscious causal formation and possible advance prediction defeat authorship, or whether temporally extended planning and macro-level control are sufficient.

sections.title: Alternative Possibilities, Determinism, and Chance
sections.rationale: This issue tests rival standards for doing otherwise and whether deterministic variation, chaotic sensitivity, or indeterminacy changes anything necessary for freedom and moral responsibility.

sections.title: Competence, Luck, and Self-Formation
sections.rationale: The parties must account for how unchosen genes, environments, neural conditions, training, and anomalous lapses bear on acquired competence, self-control, and limited self-construction.

sections.title: Moral Responsibility, Punishment, and Social Practice
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether causal explanation displaces desert while leaving only pragmatic management, or whether capacity-sensitive expectations, excuses, deterrence, and sanctions constitute ordinary responsibility.
